originalSource.version: Public release images, retrieved 2026-08-16

processing: Retrieved from the publisher's own CDN at publication resolution, resized and re-encoded to WebP for the web. Three files are rectangular crops of their source frame, listed individually below with the crop that was taken; the rest are whole frames. No recolouring, retouching or compositing was applied to any of them, and every crop is a plain rectangular selection that removes content without altering what remains. Further cropping for the hero frame is done at display time by CSS object-fit and is reversible.

Cropping is a licence question as well as a design one. CC BY 4.0 permits adaptation, and ESO's terms require the credit to stay with the image rather than requiring the frame to stay whole, so cropping is allowed — but a cropped photograph is no longer the photograph the credit line names. Each crop therefore records what was removed, and the interface continues to name the original release and photographer.

originalSource.version: Package 1.0.0; GCAT satcat source header updated 2026-06-27 22:13:02 UTC

processing: The verified v1.0.0 package preserves the immutable 2026-06-27 GCAT satcat snapshot, its exact original checksum, normalized 69,703-record products, SQLite query database, 1957-2026 annual presence, reconstruction candidates, quality ledger, schemas, build scripts, and package checksums.

python3 data/satellite-source-of-truth/scripts/verify.py validates every package artifact checksum, database schema, record and class counts, annual summaries, snapshot membership, and the package-provided deterministic reconstruction angles.

scripts/build-satellite-web-catalog.py verifies the package first, queries only the canonical SQLite database, and deterministically exports all 69,620 Earth-associated payload, rocket-body, component, and debris rows into src/data/generated/satelliteCatalog.web.json.

Completed years use GCAT-derived present_at_period_end membership. The partial 2026 view uses the package-required snapshot_present_earth_objects membership and records the two-row reconciliation difference from the generic partial-year period-end flag.

The web export preserves GCAT JCAT and available SATCAT identities, classification, owner/status, lifecycle bounds, source perigee, source apogee, source inclination, source orbit epoch, and package reconstruction angles.

For historical rows without package-precomputed angles, the export applies the package-prescribed SHA-256 algorithm keyed by the stable JCAT identifier. Runtime code never creates a second hash or random reconstruction authority.

Twenty-one latest members and 244 all-history rows with insufficient or physically invalid orbital envelopes remain catalog-only. Displayed reconstructed states are not observed, live, current, or exact positions.

originalSource.title: IMO working list of visual meteor showers, with stream identity and numbering from the IAU Meteor Data Center list of established showers
originalSource.publisher: International Meteor Organization; IAU Meteor Data Center
originalSource.version: Transcribed working-list parameters, snapshot dated 2026-08-16

processing: Twelve established showers are recorded with IAU stream number and code, parent body, solar longitude of maximum, activity interval in solar longitude, J2000 radiant at maximum, geocentric velocity, population index and nominal zenithal hourly rate.

The values were transcribed into a TypeScript module rather than retrieved as a file. There is therefore no upstream artifact to checksum and no originalSha256 is claimed; the recorded localSha256 pins the transcription, not the source.

peakWidthDays is not an IMO quantity and is not attributed to one. It is an editorial approximation of each peak's full width at half maximum, adjusted so the activity profile in src/data/tracker/meteorActivity.ts reproduces the published character of each shower. src/data/tracker/meteorShowers.ts states this in the module header.

Per R9.4, evidence class varies within a record: stream identity and elements are catalog, radiant position and peak date for a given year are analytic, and the nominal zenithal hourly rate is a forecast regardless of arriving in a catalog.
Per R9.3, the snapshot is replaced deliberately and never automatically, and a replacement records what changed.

rights.licenseOrBasis: Not established by this entry. The individual parameters are measurements of natural phenomena and are widely reproduced across published sources, but no licence grant was retrieved for the IMO working list or the IAU MDC list, and neither publisher's terms were read as part of this transcription. Resolving this means retrieving each list from its publication URL under its stated terms, checksumming the retrieved artifact, and recording the licence found there.

originalSource.title: Orbit Studio Tracker imagery policy and lunar phase composite
originalSource.version: Vector scenes drawn for the Tracker presentation rebuild, 2026-08-16

processing: Hero and card imagery is photographic and third-party; this entry covers the code that selects it, the classification vocabulary it is rendered with, and the one composite this project makes itself.

The lunar composite draws the separately registered NASA LROC mosaic and overlays the unlit portion computed for the observer's actual illuminated fraction and waxing or waning sense. A stock photograph would be the wrong shape on most nights, which the reader can check by looking up.

An earlier version of this file drew every scene as original vector art. That was replaced with licensed photography: the drawings were honest and flat, and a product whose purpose is to get somebody outside cannot afford to look like a diagram.

Every image carries an ImageryClass from src/data/tracker/imagery.ts — telescope-image, eyepiece-view, long-exposure, composite, simulation, forecast-visualisation or spacecraft-mosaic — rendered together with an observation expectation wherever the picture and the eye differ.

Phase 2 additionally requires and renders an explicit media claim (representative, event-specific, or live), origin (historical capture, current model, or live feed), capture date where applicable, and expected visual mode. None of the current Tracker assets claims to be live.

Conjunctions no longer receive a photograph. One frame of the Moon beside Venus was served for every pairing, which is the wrong planet for any pairing that is not Moon-and-Venus and the wrong lunar phase for any date but the one it was taken on. Those events are now drawn from their own ephemeris by TrackerConjunctionScene — real altitudes, azimuths, separation and Moon phase at the recommended instant — and the imagery layer returns a generic night sky to anything that still asks. The Moon-and-Venus frame still ships and is still attributed; it is simply no longer used to depict events it does not depict.

The photographs it displays are third-party and registered separately under eso-night-sky-photography and esa-hubble-planetary-photography; the lunar surface is the separately registered NASA LROC mosaic.
rights.attribution: Scene artwork by Orbit Studio. Lunar surface: NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio (LROC WAC mosaic).

release.restrictions: Every image must keep an ImageryClass and must render it, and every third-party image must render its credit on the image itself. Any future image must be registered with its own source, licence, credit and perception classification before it ships.

originalSource.title: Open-Meteo Air Quality API (Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service)
originalSource.publisher: Open-Meteo, serving Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service model output
originalSource.version: Runtime API, not a pinned snapshot; hourly aerosol_optical_depth and pm2_5

processing: Fetched from the browser at the observer’s selected location, coordinates rounded to two decimal places so observers in one model cell share a cache entry and a precise location is never used as a cache key.

Aerosol optical depth at 550 nm is the value the interface reasons from; it is converted to magnitudes of extinction (1.0857 per unit optical depth) rather than shown as a bare index, because magnitudes are the unit the observing judgement is made in. The conversion is the definition of optical depth, not a calibration.

Surface PM2.5 is used for one purpose only: a health reading, converted to the US AQI against the EPA's published PM2.5 breakpoints (2024 revision) and shown solely when the resulting category carries outdoor-exposure guidance — index 101 and above. It is never presented as sky transparency, and the two live on separate cards because they are different quantities that routinely disagree. Two limitations are stated on the card itself: the breakpoints are defined against a 24-hour average while the input is hourly, and the official index applies a NowCast weighting this does not, so a brief plume reads higher here than the published figure for the area. The cautionary wording shown with each category is the EPA's own, shortened but not reinterpreted.
Merged into the weather snapshots by timestamp with a 45-minute tolerance. A snapshot with no aerosol sample within tolerance keeps its nulls and renders as unmeasured rather than as clean air.
Requested as a separate query from the weather providers so that losing it costs one condition card rather than the whole row.

Aerosol optical depth and surface PM2.5 are never combined into a single figure. Where no aerosol model covers a location the interface shows no transparency card rather than substituting the ground-level particulate reading for it.

rights.licenseOrBasis: Open-Meteo publishes its APIs for free non-commercial use without an API key and licenses the data under CC BY 4.0. The underlying model output is the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service, whose data are available under the Copernicus licence permitting free use and redistribution with attribution. The endpoint sends access-control-allow-origin: *, so direct browser use is the intended access pattern.
rights.attribution: Aerosol and particulate data from Open-Meteo, derived from the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service, licensed CC BY 4.0. Rendered in the Tracker conditions caption and in the data-and-privacy panel.

release.restrictions: Attribution must remain visible wherever aerosol figures are shown. Optical depth must not be presented as a smoke concentration, and surface particulate must not be presented as sky transparency. Caching must stay keyed by model cell and never by user. If Orbit Studio ever becomes commercial, Open-Meteo’s non-commercial terms must be re-reviewed before this remains on the free path.

originalSource.title: NOAA SWPC OVATION aurora nowcast and planetary K-index products
originalSource.version: Runtime API, not a pinned snapshot; ovation_aurora_latest.json, noaa-planetary-k-index-forecast.json, planetary_k_index_1m.json

processing: Tracker's second runtime external request, and the only one that is not per-location: NOAA publishes one global grid, so the request carries no coordinates and every observer shares one fetch. Nothing about the observer is transmitted.

The OVATION grid is parsed into a typed array indexed by whole degrees. NOAA’s published quantity — the probability of visible aurora in percent — is carried through unmodified and is attributed to NOAA wherever it is shown. Tracker applies no model of its own on top of it.

Three horizons are kept apart rather than merged: the OVATION nowcast (valid roughly half an hour), the three-day planetary K-index forecast, and nothing at all beyond that. The interface refuses to speak past the third.
The nowcast and the K-index are separate queries so that a dropped request for one retries without discarding the other. Neither response is stored; both are held in memory for the session only.

Freshness is read from the product’s own forecast time rather than from a chosen interval: a grid past its forecast time is ageing, and past a further grace period is stale. A stale grid stops producing a probability, an outlook and a ranking weight entirely, and what NOAA last reported is carried separately so the interface can show it as history rather than as advice.

The ranking weight Tracker derives from NOAA’s probability is an editorial transformation and is declared as one in code (auroraRankingStrength returns editorial: true with a stated basis). NOAA publishes a probability of visible aurora; it does not publish an opinion about whether that beats Saturn.

Whether aurora could be seen from a location, as distinct from being overhead at it, is derived by Tracker rather than read from NOAA. OVATION reports the probability of aurora overhead; emission occurs at altitude, so it clears the horizon from far outside the oval. SWPC publishes exactly this as the aurora viewline, but only as rendered rasters under /experimental/images/aurora_dashboard/ — there is no coordinate form in /json/, /experimental/json/ or /products/ — so it is not consumed. Instead the horizon reach is computed as R*arccos(R/(R+h)) and the apparent elevation by spherical geometry, with h taken from NOAA's published range of 80-500 km (100 km for the bright lower border, 400 km for tall red emission). The resulting angle and direction are Tracker's derivation and are never attributed to NOAA.

Copy pass: the sentences Tracker builds from this data were rewritten for plainness without changing what they claim. Nowcast-versus-forecast wording, the expiry language, the attribution of NOAA's probability and the disclaimer that the derived horizon angle is Tracker's own are all preserved verbatim in meaning.

NOAA’s data policy and the SWPC service terms permit free use and redistribution of these products with acknowledgment. The endpoints send access-control-allow-origin: * and a one-minute cache header, so direct browser use is the intended access pattern and no proxy or key is required.
rights.attribution: Aurora nowcast (OVATION) and planetary K-index from the NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center (public domain). Rendered in the Tracker conditions caption and in the data-and-privacy panel.

release.restrictions: NOAA acknowledgment must remain visible wherever aurora figures are shown, and no endorsement may be implied. Any percentage shown must be NOAA's published figure, unmodified and attributed; a value Tracker derives from it may not be presented as a probability or as NOAA's. Nothing beyond the three-day K-index horizon may be presented as a forecast. If the operator ever adds a proxy, its caching must respect the one-minute publication cadence. The derived horizon-visibility angle and look direction are Tracker's own geometry, not a NOAA product, and must not be presented as NOAA's viewline.

originalSource.title: Photon geocoder over OpenStreetMap data
originalSource.version: Runtime API, not a pinned snapshot; queried per search

processing: Place search runs from the browser against a public Photon instance. Queries are the text the reader typed; no identifier accompanies them and nothing is stored.
Requests are debounced so a free service is not asked for a result per keystroke, and searches shorter than three characters are not sent at all.

Results are re-ranked locally to favour the categories an observer means — campsites, parks, reserves, summits, viewpoints and trailheads above street addresses — because the campground case is the one the location contract exists for.
A coordinate pair typed into the same field is parsed locally and never sent anywhere, which is the fallback for a site too remote to be in any database.
The adapter declares its cost as public-no-fee and the router will not return a cost-bearing geocoder on the free path, enforced the same way as for weather.

Results without a `name` are labelled from housenumber and street rather than discarded. Requiring a name dropped every street address, which is why a valid full address reported no matches while queries near a named building resolved to the building instead.

rights.licenseOrBasis: The underlying data is OpenStreetMap under ODbL 1.0 and attribution is rendered in the Tracker sources detail, so redistribution of results is not in question. What is unresolved is production reliance on a courtesy public endpoint: no usage agreement has been sought with the instance operator, and a product sending real traffic to a free community service should either have one or run its own. Resolving it means either an agreement, a self-hosted Photon, or a paid provider — and the last of those is barred from the free path by the cost rule.
rights.attribution: Place search © OpenStreetMap contributors, ODbL 1.0. Geocoding by Photon.

release.restrictions: OpenStreetMap attribution must remain visible. Searches must stay debounced and must not carry a user identifier. No cost-bearing geocoder may be added to the free path. This entry must not be marked verified until production use of the endpoint is put on a footing the operator has agreed to.

originalSource.title: MET Norway Locationforecast 2.0 and the US National Weather Service API
originalSource.publisher: Norwegian Meteorological Institute; NOAA National Weather Service
originalSource.version: Runtime API, not a pinned snapshot; queried live per observing location

processing: This is Tracker's first runtime external request. Forecasts are fetched from the browser at the observer's selected location and are never bundled, stored on a server, or attributed to a user.

Requests are keyed and cached by forecast grid cell, coordinates rounded to two decimal places, rather than by user. Rounding is both a caching requirement of the providers and a deliberate limit on the precision of the location that is transmitted.

Routing prefers the National Weather Service inside the United States for its finer grid and falls back to MET Norway globally. Both are declared public-no-fee; the router will not return a cost-bearing adapter on the free path.

Provider schemas are normalised into one internal ConditionSnapshot. MET Norway's fog area fraction is converted to a nominal visibility in metres, which is the only place a provider's value is reinterpreted rather than renamed.
No smoke or air-quality source is fetched. Those snapshot fields stay null, and the model treats null as unknown rather than as clean air.

rights.licenseOrBasis: MET Norway Locationforecast is published under CC BY 4.0 and the National Weather Service API is US Government work in the public domain, so redistribution of the *data* is not in question. What is unresolved is compliance with the providers' identification requirement: both ask a caller to send a User-Agent identifying the application, and a browser cannot — User-Agent is a forbidden header name in the Fetch standard, so the browser discards it and sends its own. Verified empirically against an echo service. Resolving this means routing through a caching proxy that can set the header, which is a server and therefore a running cost.
rights.attribution: Weather data from MET Norway, licensed CC BY 4.0. Forecast data from the US National Weather Service (public domain). Both attributions are rendered in the Tracker conditions detail.

release.restrictions: Attribution must remain visible in the conditions detail. Caching must stay keyed by grid cell and never by user. The identification gap above must not be marked resolved until requests carry an identifying User-Agent. No cost-bearing weather or geocoding provider may be added to the free path.

processing: Downloaded from the Wikimedia upload host at publication resolution (1920×1080, 6,818,693 bytes, SHA-256 ae083f54063cb4ec7bcb30aa6ba959bab6854c04c781d8c2491d347bd470c1b7). Rescaled to 1280×720 and re-encoded VP9 at CRF 36, taking it from 6.8 MB to 594 kB; the audio track was dropped, since the clip is used muted and shipping an unused stream is dead weight. The poster is frame one of the same clip, encoded to WebP.

No frames were altered, recoloured, composited or reordered. The footage is a real historical capture and is presented as representative natural-speed footage, never as a live feed or the reader's current sky.

The licence was verified against this individual file rather than inherited from the host. The Commons API returns LicenseShortName CC0, UsageTerms "Creative Commons Zero, Public Domain Dedication", Artist Bautsch, Credit "Own work". Wikimedia hosts files under many different licences and one file's terms say nothing about the next.

rights.licenseOrBasis: Creative Commons Zero 1.0 Universal public-domain dedication. Attribution is rendered anyway: the reader is being shown someone else's night, and saying whose is a matter of honesty rather than compliance.
